summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds. Alagoas stands under that national framework: state law does not displace the constitutional and federal provisions described below.

After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

Killing risk is measurable and Alagoas is recorded in the national tally. ANTRA's 9th annual dossier, reported by SBT News on 26 January 2026, counted 80 trans and travesti people killed across Brazil in 2025, a fall of roughly 34% year-on-year, leaving the country first in world rankings; the victims were overwhelmingly travestis and trans women, killed with extreme violence, and Alagoas accounted for 2 of those 80 killings. The preceding dossier, reported by CNN Brasil on 27 January 2025, counted 122 people killed in 2024, 16% below 2023, with Alagoas accounting for 6 of them.

Detention carries a specific regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions.
tangentialFactors:
Brazil has ranked first in the world for the killing of trans people for a 16th consecutive year, according to ANTRA's 2024 dossier. The 122 victims of that year and the 80 of 2025 were mostly young Black women, many from the Northeast, and the crimes were marked by extreme violence, a profile that bears on where and to whom risk concentrates rather than on any single state.

Nightlife carries documented targeting. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. The incident is a single-city data point and no comparable Alagoas source is available.

Hostility also surfaces through the ballot. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Prison practice diverges from the national detention rules. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.
localsOnly:
Protection machinery has widened for residents. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Residents change legal gender without surgery following the Supreme Federal Tribunal's 2018 removal of the surgical requirement, and family matters involving same-sex spouses are handled under the nationwide marriage and spousal-visa rules.

Trans people resident in Brazil participate in municipal officeholding at rising rates, but candidacy at the October 2024 cycle drew death threats and intimidation against close to 1,000 transgender candidates nationwide.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Alagoas-specific source in the inventory reports enforcement of the SOGI hate-crime provisions within the state, prosecution rates, or outcomes of complaints filed there; the two homicide counts for Alagoas (2 in 2025, 6 in 2024) are the only state-level figures available.

Whether Alagoas has its own state anti-discrimination statute or LGBTI policy, separate from the federal framework, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

ANTRA's counting methodology, its definition of a confirmed killing, and the basis for the year-on-year percentage changes are not stated in the two reports cited, so the totals should be read as the organisation's own tally rather than an official statistic.

No source addresses airport or border screening of gender markers on passports in Brazil, or how a mismatch between passport data and presentation is handled at entry; the April 2026 legal guide speaks only to the national operation of gender-marker and spousal-visa rules.

The Rio de Janeiro prison census describes one state's system in 2021 and cannot be assumed to reflect Alagoas correctional facilities, for which no data is present in this inventory.
